strengths: Clear, well-motivated, and cohesive narrative: The paper systematically examines actor parameterization and architecture in on-policy continuous control, framing discretized categorical policies through the lens of classification-style cross-entropy optimization.

Rigorous experimental design and clean 2x2 factorial ablations: The evaluation spans MuJoCo locomotion, 10 ManiSkill state-based manipulation tasks, and 5 vision-based manipulation tasks. The 2x2 comparison (RN-D, RN-C, MLP-D, MLP-C) cleanly disentangles the distinct contributions of the network architecture and the action discretization.

Insightful diagnostic experiments: The 'loss-swap' ablation (Appendix C.2 / Figure 6b) is particularly commendable, as it isolates the effect of the categorical likelihood/cross-entropy optimization from the action discretization itself.

Thorough empirical analysis: The manuscript includes gradient variance measurements, SNR analysis, actor capacity scaling, action bin granularity sweeps, and wall-clock comparisons against off-policy baselines.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Both core components—factorized continuous action discretization for on-policy RL (Tang & Agrawal, 2020; Zhu et al., 2024) and Pre-LN residual MLP architectures (e.g., SimBa, BroNet)—are existing concepts from prior literature, making the technical contribution primarily an empirical synthesis and validation.

Apples-to-oranges aspect of Proposition 4.1: The gradient variance bound compares $\nabla_\mu \log \pi^c$ in $\mathbb{R}^m$ against $\nabla_z \log \pi^d$ in $\mathbb{R}^{mK}$. Because logits and continuous action means operate in fundamentally different metric spaces with different dimensions, comparing Euclidean norms of these gradients in toy REINFORCE should be interpreted with caution regarding actual parameter updates in deep networks.

Degradation under high bin counts: As shown in Figure 6(d) and Appendix C.4, performance falls off significantly when bin count exceeds ~100 bins. This reveals a fundamental limitation of uniform discretization for continuous control tasks requiring sub-millimeter precision, which the paper acknowledges but leaves unresolved.
Minor presentation redundancies: Figure 6 in Section 7 and Figure 7 in Appendix C are identical figures repeated verbatim, which could be streamlined.

strengths: Clean empirical motivation and structure: The paper systematically revisits policy parameterization for on-policy RL (PPO), connecting action discretization to classification-style cross-entropy objectives that mirror recent trends in value learning and LLM fine-tuning.

Thorough factorial ablation study: The experiments isolate the effects of the regularized residual architecture and categorical discretization via a full 2x2 comparison (RN-D, RN-C, MLP-D, MLP-C) across standard MuJoCo locomotion and 15 ManiSkill manipulation tasks (both state-based and vision-based).

Insightful loss-swap ablation: The experiment in Section 7 / Appendix C.2—where categorical logits predict an expected action optimized under Gaussian likelihood—effectively disentangles the representational effect of discretization from the optimization geometry induced by the cross-entropy objective.

Empirical rigor: Experiments report results over multiple random seeds with 95% stratified bootstrap confidence intervals, full per-task learning curves, and wall-clock comparisons against off-policy baselines (TD3, TD-MPC2).
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic and architectural novelty: The core components—uniform per-dimension action discretization (Tang & Agrawal, 2020) and pre-LayerNorm residual MLP feedforward blocks (standard Transformer FFN / SimBa / BroNet)—are existing techniques. While the empirical validation is solid, the technical contribution lies primarily in recombining known architectural practices.

Limitations of the theoretical variance analysis: Proposition 4.1 compares the variance of gradients with respect to the distribution parameters (the continuous mean vector $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^m$ versus the discrete logit vector $z \in \mathbb{R}^{mK}$) under an unbaselined one-step REINFORCE setting with constant return. Because these parameters live in different spaces with differing dimensions ($m$ vs. $mK$) and learning dynamics, and because practical updates propagate through deep network weights $\theta$, this comparison does not directly translate to the actual parameter gradient variance $\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\text{PPO}}$.

Absence of direct comparisons with prior discretized continuous-control methods: The empirical evaluation compares solely against continuous Gaussian actors and plain MLP discretized actors, omitting structured discrete baselines from prior literature such as ordinal categorical policies (Tang & Agrawal, 2020) or unimodal/Poisson policies (Zhu et al., 2024).

Sensitivity to discretization granularity: As highlighted in Section 7 and Figure 6(d), performance drops sharply when the action bin resolution increases ($K > 100$). This sensitivity to bin count indicates that the approach may struggle in continuous control domains requiring very fine, high-precision actuation without specialized tokenization or hierarchical discretization.

strengths: Clean and well-structured empirical design: The 2x2 factorial evaluation comparing MLP vs. Regularized Network (RN) crossed with Continuous Gaussian vs. Discretized Categorical (MLP-C, MLP-D, RN-C, RN-D) cleanly isolates the individual and synergistic effects of the network architecture and the categorical action parameterization.

Extensive and diverse evaluation: The method is validated across 20 distinct environments spanning MuJoCo locomotion, low-dimensional state-based ManiSkill tasks, and visual (RGB) ManiSkill tasks, demonstrating consistent performance and sample-efficiency gains (notably solving StackCube-v1 where Gaussian baselines struggle).

Insightful diagnostic experiments: The loss-swap ablation (Section 7 / Appendix C.2), which keeps the discretized action output but optimizes via expected mean squared error instead of cross-entropy, provides clear evidence that the categorical likelihood/cross-entropy optimization geometry—rather than mere action binning—is central to the observed performance gains.

Detailed analysis of training dynamics: The paper provides meaningful empirical measurements of gradient signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), empirical policy gradient variance throughout training, and sensitivity analyses regarding actor capacity and the number of discretization bins ($K$).
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Discretizing continuous action spaces with factorized categorical heads for on-policy RL is already well established (e.g., Tang & Agrawal, 2020; Zhu et al., 2024), and utilizing pre-LayerNorm residual MLPs is adopted from standard deep learning and recent RL architectures (e.g., SimBa, BroNet). The primary contribution is empirical synthesis rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic mechanism.

Limitations of the theoretical comparison in Proposition 4.1: The variance comparison directly compares the squared gradient norm with respect to the action mean vector $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^m$ against the logits $z \in \mathbb{R}^{mK}$. Comparing Euclidean parameter gradient norms across parameterizations with differing dimensions ($m$ vs. $mK$) and different metric tensors can be misleading, as parameter scale and effective step size in probability space differ substantially.

Scalability to high-precision and coordinated control: Factorized independent categorical distributions ignore inter-dimensional correlations. Furthermore, the bin scaling analysis (Figure 6d) reveals noticeable performance degradation when the bin count exceeds $\sim 100$, indicating vulnerability when high continuous control precision is required.

Algorithmic breadth: The investigation is restricted exclusively to PPO. Evaluating whether these benefits transfer consistently to other on-policy policy gradient variants (such as PPG, TRPO, or A2C) would strengthen the generality of the conclusions.

Minor manuscript layout redundancy: Figure 6 in Section 7 is duplicated verbatim as Figure 7 in Appendix C, and the text in Appendix C repeatedly references Figure 7 instead of maintaining a streamlined flow.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The paper conducts experiments across multiple domains (Gym locomotion, 10 state-based ManiSkill tasks, and 5 vision-based ManiSkill tasks) and validates the findings across three different on-policy algorithms (PPO, TRPO, and SPO).

Thorough ablation and factorial design: The 2x2 comparison across architectures (MLP vs. Regularized Network) and action spaces (Continuous Gaussian vs. Discretized Categorical) cleanly isolates the individual and synergistic contributions of the network design and categorical parameterization.

Insightful loss-swap experiment: The ablation in Section C.2—where discrete logits are used to form an expected action trained under a Gaussian log-likelihood—provides convincing evidence that the cross-entropy-like optimization geometry, rather than discretization alone, drives much of the empirical improvement.

Clear presentation and execution: The paper is well-structured, easy to follow, provides detailed training throughput/wall-clock analyses, and investigates practical questions such as actor capacity scaling and sensitivity to bin granularity.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Discretizing continuous action spaces with factorized categorical distributions for on-policy RL was previously introduced and studied by Tang & Agrawal (2020) and Zhu et al. (2024), while pre-LayerNorm residual MLP blocks are standard in modern deep RL (e.g., SimBa, BroNet) and NLP. The primary contribution is empirical and confirmatory rather than conceptual.

Apples-to-oranges theoretical comparison in Proposition 4.1: Comparing the gradient variance with respect to the continuous mean parameter $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^m$ against the gradient with respect to categorical logits $z \in \mathbb{R}^{mK}$ compares quantities across different parameter dimensions and arbitrary coordinate scalings. The variance of the actual policy parameter gradients $\nabla_\theta$ depends strongly on the network Jacobian $\partial z / \partial \theta$ versus $\partial \mu / \partial \theta$, making the bound somewhat artificial.

Sensitivity and scaling limitations with respect to bin resolution: As demonstrated in Appendix C.4, performance degrades sharply when bin counts exceed $K \approx 100$. For tasks requiring fine continuous motor adjustments, the tradeoff between quantization error and categorical optimization difficulty remains an open challenge not fully addressed by uniform binning.

Factorized independence assumption: Assuming strict conditional independence across action dimensions ($a \sim \prod_i \pi_i(a_i|s)$) ignores inter-action correlations, which can become problematic in complex, tightly coupled multi-DoF robotic manipulation tasks.

strengths: Thorough empirical evaluation across 20 distinct environments spanning Gym locomotion, state-based ManiSkill, and vision-based ManiSkill manipulation tasks, showing consistent empirical gains across multiple on-policy algorithms (PPO, TRPO, SPO).

Well-designed ablation studies, including a complete 2x2 factorial comparison (MLP-C, MLP-D, RN-C, RN-D) and a loss-swap experiment (Appendix C.2) that isolates the impact of the categorical likelihood objective from discrete binning.
Comprehensive empirical diagnostics, including gradient variance tracking, gradient signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) across training, and detailed wall-clock throughput measurements.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic originality: The proposed method is essentially a combination of previously known components—specifically, per-dimension uniform action discretization (Tang & Agrawal, 2020) and pre-LayerNorm residual MLP blocks commonly used in recent deep RL architecture works (such as SimBa and BroNet). The paper does not introduce a new architectural module or training objective.

Theoretical comparison in Proposition 4.1 has conceptual limitations: The proposition compares the gradient norm with respect to the mean vector $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^m$ against the gradient norm with respect to the logits $z \in \mathbb{R}^{mK}$. These gradient vectors lie in parameter spaces of different dimensions ($m$ vs. $mK$). Directly comparing their Euclidean norms in a toy tabular setting overlooks how gradients backpropagate through the shared network parameters $\theta$ via the Jacobian matrices $\partial \mu / \partial \theta$ versus $\partial z / \partial \theta$.

Degradation under fine discretization remains unresolved: As shown in Figure 7(d) and Appendix C.4, policy performance deteriorates significantly when the number of bins $K$ exceeds 100. Because the policy ignores the ordinal structure of the discretized action bins, it cannot scale cleanly to fine-grained control without performance loss, which was precisely the motivation for prior ordinal and unimodal discrete parameterizations (e.g., Tang & Agrawal, 2020; Zhu et al., 2024).
Incomplete text and editorial polish: The Abstract ends with an incomplete dangling sentence ('We release our code at'), indicating an unedited placeholder and a lack of final proofreading.

strengths: Clear motivation and unifying perspective: The paper provides a compelling motivation connecting continuous action discretization to classification-style cross-entropy optimization, drawing insightful parallels to recent findings in categorical value function learning and RLHF for language models.

Comprehensive and rigorous empirical evaluation: The proposed RN-D is evaluated across 5 Gym locomotion tasks, 10 state-based ManiSkill tasks, and 5 vision-based ManiSkill tasks across three different on-policy algorithms (PPO, TRPO, and SPO), demonstrating consistent gains in sample efficiency and final performance.

Well-designed ablations: The 2x2 factorial comparison between network architectures (MLP vs. RN) and policy parameterizations (Gaussian vs. Discrete) cleanly isolates the source of the improvements. Furthermore, the loss-swap ablation (Appendix C.2) is particularly illuminating in showing that the categorical likelihood/cross-entropy geometry—rather than discretization alone—drives the empirical performance.

Practical utility: The paper thoroughly measures sample throughput and wall-clock time, demonstrating that factorized categorical discretization introduces negligible computational overhead while scaling favorably with network capacity.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Discretizing continuous action spaces with factorized categorical distributions is an established concept (e.g., Tang & Agrawal, 2020; Zhu et al., 2024), as are pre-LayerNorm residual MLP architectures (e.g., SimBa, BroNet). The core contribution is largely an empirical synthesis and design recipe rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic mechanism.

Theoretical comparison caveats: Proposition 4.1 compares the gradient variance with respect to the mean vector $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^m$ against the gradient with respect to logits $z \in \mathbb{R}^{mK}$. Because these gradients live in different parameter spaces of different dimensionalities and interact differently with optimization hyperparameters (e.g., learning rate and Adam second moments), comparing gradient norm bounds directly has limited practical implications.

Degradation under fine discretization: As demonstrated in Appendix C.4 (Figure 7d / 8d), policy performance drops sharply when the number of bins exceeds 100. This indicates a tension between action precision and optimization stability, which may limit applicability in domains requiring fine-grained continuous control.

Minor presentation issues: The abstract abruptly ends with an incomplete sentence ('We release our code at'), and minor citation anomalies exist in the text (e.g., 'Lee et al., 2024; Lee et al.' on page 6).
